Q: How do contrastive objectives and hard negatives shape embedding behavior?
A:
An embedding model learns a representation under its training objective; closeness is not an inherent property of language. Contrastive training pulls selected positive pairs together and separates negatives under a specified loss and sampling policy.

Hard negatives can teach subtle distinctions but mislabeled negatives can repel genuinely relevant evidence. Match the training pair construction to query and document roles and keep held-out evaluation separate. Evaluate important slices after adaptation because improvement on average can erase a domain-specific distinction.
Why: 'Refund allowed' and 'refund not allowed' share many words but have opposite applicability. Reviewed hard negatives can expose that error, while treating a valid exception as an irrelevant negative would damage the desired ranking.
Risk: A high similarity score is not a calibrated probability of answer support.
Trade: Domain adaptation helps when errors justify it and labels are reliable.
